draft:
A hive splits mainly as a natural means of increase. When adult bee ranks rise fast, nectar is ample, spring air is mild, and the nest is tight, egg-laying space can fall. Bees then raise fresh queens. The present queen flies away with a large share of bees, while a virgin queen stays. This eases pressure and lets the bee family spread. It can arise in a well-run apiary; it is a natural drive, rather than a mark of weak care.

Within the 14-day lead-up, seek wax queen cups, then eggs in these cups, then larvae amid rich jelly. Cups are usually at frame base and edges. A cup can be idle, yet several charged cups indicate serious swarm intent. As cells lengthen, creating large peanut-like queen cells, and then gain wax caps, flight may be very near. A prime cast may leave as the first cells are capped, given fair air.

At the same time, the nest may seem jammed: bees blanket frames, nectar fills cells needed for eggs, and wax building is brisk. Egg laying may shrink. The queen may seem slimmer, as her feed can be cut ahead of flight. Bees may mass at the entrance and hang beneath the hive in warm air. This can signal heat relief as well; thus queen-cell facts carry greater weight.

An egg in a queen cup gives, at best, near 8 days until sealing. As sealing nears, a prime cast can leave at any time. Keep a dated hive diary; cell age, egg presence, and caps give a far safer guide than hive size by itself.

A hive swarms as a natural means by which bees spread. In spring, a rapidly rising adult-bee mass, ample nectar, warm days, and a nest with scant vacant cells can trigger this drive. During the 14-day lead-up, inspect each frame with care. Seek queen cups, mainly at frame base and side rims. Empty cups are very usual and may mean little. Eggs, larvae, and rich white jelly within several cups are far clearer signs that swarm plans are active. These cells lengthen, gain a peanut-like shape, and are then sealed. After sealing, the main swarm may depart in fair, calm weather very rapidly.

Further signs can include a nest packed with bees, brisk wax making, nectar filling cells, and less egg laying by the queen. The queen may appear slimmer, since bees may feed her less prior to flight. Bees may hang in a mass at the hive entry or beneath the hive during warm days. Seedlings go pale and leggy mainly from weak light. A window sill may look bright, yet its light level is far below that in open air. Glass also blocks part of the light. In a warm room, stems can extend fast while leaves cannot make ample food. This gives long, thin stems, wide gaps between leaves, and a faded green color. Crowding can make this worse.

Before the next sowing:

- Start a bit later if days are dark.
- Keep trays at a bright, cool window, very near the glass, but not against it.
- Best: add an LED plant lamp. Hang it 5–10 cm above the leaves and run it 14–16 h daily. Raise it as plants grow.
- Keep the growing mix evenly damp, not wet, and avoid excess heat.
- Give each seedling room; move it into a larger pot before roots pack tight.
- Once the first set of real leaves forms, add a mild plant feed, as the label says.

Wet-Season Lamp Notes

Get a sealed, waterproof front lamp plus a red rear lamp. Choose a metal or tough nylon case, a rubber-covered charge port, and no bare metal contacts. Avoid cheap lamps whose charge flap hangs open.

Salt and water demand care. After each wet run, wash off salt: use fresh water, then dry the lamp and mount. Let the charge port dry before power-up. A small dab of grease on mount bolts can help ward off rust.

A rip is a fast, narrow flow of surf wash moving back out from sand. Surf and wind push lots of water up a sandy bank; that water has to run back out. A gap in sand bars can focus this outflow into a hard pull. It is not a sink: its main risk is carrying you far out and tiring you if you fight it.

From sand, look for a long, dark or oddly calm strip amid surf, with foam or bits of flotsam drifting outward. Also watch for surf booming on both flanks but not in its midpart. Such marks can shift fast, so ask surf patrol about local risk.

If a rip pulls you, stay calm, float, and signal for aid. Do not swim in hard against its flow. Aim left or right, across its flow, until surf is pushing you in; if this is not working, float until its pull drops, signal, and work in with incoming surf. If a pal is in a rip, call surf patrol or local aid. Do not go in if that puts you at risk.

That water must flow back out, often through a low gap in a sandbar, forming a swift outward run. It will not drag you down, but it can carry you far from land and sap your vigor if you fight it.

From land, look for a dark, calm strip amid rough surf. You may spot foam, sand, or bits of drift moving outward. A gap with surf crashing on both sides can hint at a rip. Ask a local surf patrol about risky spots.

If a rip grabs you, stay calm. Float, lift an arm, and call for aid. Do not swim hard toward land. Swim across its flow until you pass its pull, then turn toward land. If that is too hard, float until its pull drops, then swim in. If you spot a pal in a rip, call 911 or flag down a surf patrol. Toss a float if you can; do not go in without a flotation aid and skill.

draft:
Two split tries do not show poor skill. Use low fire, keep things moving, and quit before boiling.

Use 2 egg yolks, 240 ml milk, 2 tbsp honey, plus 2 tsp cornflour. If you seek more sweetness, use 1 more tsp honey.

Whisk yolks, honey, cornflour, plus 60 ml milk in cool pot until smooth. In second pot, bring leftover milk to tiny bubbles round rim; no simmering. Drip hot milk into yolk mix, whisking nonstop. Begin with only few drops, then use thin, slow pour.

Return mix to pot. Set it over low fire. Stir nonstop, with whisk or silicone spoon, so no bit sits still on pot bottom. Do not permit bubbling. Once mix turns visibly thicker, keep stirring for 20 to 30 sec, then pull pot off fire. It will firm further while it cools.

Pour through sieve into cool bowl. Put film directly over top, then chill. If it looks slightly lumpy, sieve it right off fire; do not keep it on fire in hope of fixing it.

Key point: yolks split if too hot. Tiny bubbles round pot rim mean it is nearly too hot, so pull it off fire then.

draft:
Two split lots do not imply poor skill. Use low fire, stir nonstop, plus stop well before boil.

Put 2 egg yolks, 2 tbsp sugar, 2 tsp cornflour, plus 60 ml milk in cool pot. Whisk until silky. Bring 180 ml milk in second pot to tiny bubbles round its edge. Do not let it simmer.

Drip hot milk into yolk mix, whisking nonstop. Begin drop by drop; then pour in thin trickle. This slow step keeps yolks from splitting.

Put mix over lowest fire. Stir nonstop, getting into pot rim plus bottom. Keep it below simmer: no bubbles. Once it clings to spoon, cook 20 sec more, then lift pot from fire. If you own thermometer, lift it off when it hits 80 C. Do not let it top 83 C.

Push it through sieve into cool bowl. Put film directly on top, then chill.

If it turns lumpy, lift it off fire right off. Stir briskly, then sieve. Do not keep it on fire.

draft:
Why this flight occurs

In spring, brood production rises quickly. If worker numbers outgrow room in hive, old-queen scent does not spread well through brood nest. Crowding, too few open cells, honey plugging brood comb, poor hive cooling, or declining queen scent can tip colony into reproductive mode. Workers then produce new queens. Old queen departs with numerous workers, seeking new home; those left behind grow one new queen. It is routine colony reproduction, not solely poor hive keeping.

Clues in prior fortnight

Look inside every 5 to 7 d, with minimal smoke, during good flying conditions. Do not rely on cups only: empty, dry cups occur in numerous colonies. Risk rises when cups hold an egg, then tiny white grub in jelly, chiefly if cells sit on lower or side comb rims. Multiple long, ridged queen cells, not just one or two, show serious intent.

Brood comb often looks plugged, with little open room for eggs because honey fills cells. Egg output from old queen might shrink. More drones could be present. Bees could cluster under entrance or on hive front in hot evenings; this hints congestion, though it does not prove an imminent exit. Old queen often becomes lighter because workers feed her less, so she can fly.

Sequence is useful. Queen cells begin with eggs, then tiny grubs, then sealed cells. Once cells become sealed, old queen could leave very soon, frequently before first new queen comes out. Cold, wet, or windy spells could hold things up. Therefore, if you see occupied cells plus congestion, promptly put in more empty comb, split colony, or follow your club's tried control method.

## What a soot pro will do

A first call often starts with a chat. Your soot pro asks what work did occur, what you plan to burn, and if smoke, soot, or odd odours did occur in past use. Say if gas or oil is also in use; its rules can vary.

A good pro looks at both room and stack. Indoors, this may span ash pit, throat, smoke-path lining, surround, and signs of damp, cracks, or old soot. Outdoors, if roof footing is sound, it may span stack brickwork, pots, cowls, flashing, and roof risks. A lamp, mirror, or small camera can look up a long run for bird-built blocks, old mortar, tar, or partial blocks.

To limit dust, cloths go around flooring and soft goods; a board or cloth may go across your old opening. A high-suction vac runs by that opening. Brush heads on long rods go up from indoors, or down from roof-top, to knock soot and tar off path walls. Dust and bits fall into a catch area and go into a vac. A good pro works slowly, using rods and brush forms to suit your stack.

On an old spot, a first job may pull out far more than soot. A bird block, loose mortar, a fall of brick, or hard tar may halt work. Your pro should flag any fault and say what must occur prior to use. Do not burn logs or coal until all vital work is put right.

At wrap-up, ask for a short account: what was found, if your smoke path is fit for normal burning, and any work still on hold. Also ask about a CO alarm, dry logs, and how soon to book again. Many wood or coal spots call for an annual soot job; much use, damp logs, or coal may call for a shorter gap.

### Why a colony swarms

A swarm lets one strong nest become two nests. The old queen leaves with a large band of workers and drones to seek a new home. Back at the old nest, a young queen takes over.

Swarm prep tends to start when brood output and nectar flow make adult bee numbers surge. A packed brood nest, lots of young workers, warm days, and an old queen can add pressure. Nectar or pollen stored where the queen needs to lay can worsen the problem.

Lack of room can help push a colony toward swarming, yet room alone does not cause every swarm. The key event occurs when workers start to rear new queens.

### Clues over 14 days

**About 14 to 10 days ahead**

- Small queen cups show up, often at lower comb edges.
- Empty cups alone may mean no more than normal colony work.
- Eggs placed in several cups are a much stronger alert.

**About 10 to 6 days ahead**

- Eggs hatch and larvae get royal jelly.
- Cups grow into long queen cells.
- The brood nest may look packed.
- Nectar and pollen may take up cells that the queen would use for eggs.
- The old queen may lay fewer eggs.
- More drones may be seen.

**Near 8 days after an egg goes down**

- Queen cells get capped.
- The first swarm often leaves soon after the first queen cell gets capped.
- Cold, wet weather, or strong wind can hold the swarm back.

**Last few days**

- Bees may mass at the entrance, hang below the floor, or form a beard on hot days.
- Forager flow may seem lower.
- The nest may sound more restless or loud.
- Bees may gorge on honey before departure.

### What matters most

Do not judge from cups alone. Look for eggs or larvae in queen cells, then note when cells get capped. Check each brood comb, as swarm cells often occur at lower or outer edges. Once several queen cells hold eggs or larvae, use a swarm-control plan at once.

draft:
Pricing craft-fair work

Pricing craft-fair work is a balancing act: pay all outlay, pay for your skill, and stay within what fair folk will pay. Start with math; try it at fairs.

1. Find your full cost

For a usual item, add:

- raw goods
- packing, tags, and card-app cuts
- a portion of stall cost, trip, food, tax, and tool upkeep
- your hourly pay × hours of labor

Full cost = all of that.

2. Add profit

Your sum must sit above full cost. If it only hits full cost, no profit is on hand for growth, flaws, or slow days.

Start by adding 25% to 100% of full cost. A low add-on can fit quick work with lots of units; a high add-on can fit original, skill-rich, or long-hour work.

3. Scan local norms

Look at work akin to yours at fairs, studios, and shops. Jot down sums by size, finish, and skill. This is a solid signal, not a law. Do not copy a low sum from a hobbyist who skips labor or stall costs.

4. Build a sum stair

Put out low-sum add-ons, mid-sum main work, and a few high-sum showstops. Folks can buy at various sums, and your top skill is on show. A stall full of only tiny bargains can pull your sums down; a stall with only costly work may limit buys.

5. Put tags on all work

Hold sums in sync across your stall, app, and social spots. Do not cut a sum on a whim. If you allow a fair-day cut for flawed stock or a multi-item buy, plan it prior.

6. Log and adjust

At fairs, log what sold, at what sum, and how fast. Log kind words, pushback, and how many folks ask for info.

Do not cut sums in panic following a slow fair. Bad rain, poor stall location, or a wrong crowd can hurt sales. Look at 3 to 5 fairs with akin crowds, and shift sums by 5% to 10%.

7. Watch stock and buys

All stock gone fast at full sum: lift sums a bit, or bring additional stock.

Few buys, lots of looking, and no talk of quality: cut costs, add a low-sum item, or shift how your work is shown.

Lots of kind talk but few buys: folks may like it but not fit your fair's budget.

Do not try discounts as your first fix. Find out if form, tag info, booth layout, or fair fit is at fault.

A math run

Raw goods $12; labor: 2 hours at $20 = $40; stall and trip part $8; packing and card-app cuts $5. Full cost: $65. Add 40% profit: $91. A $90 tag is a sound start, if similar work and fair traffic back it up.

A sound sum is not a random gut call. It pays you now, funds stock and tools, and suits a known kind of folk. Start with solid math, put tags out with calm, and adjust from logs, not from fright.

draft:
## No-Split Custard

Two bad runs do not say you lack skill. This path has a big margin.

For a small bowl:

- 300 g full-fat milk
- 3 yolks
- 60 g sugar
- 25 g cornstarch
- 1 pinch salt
- 1 tsp vanilla

1. Start with a cool, sturdy pan. Add yolks, sugar, cornstarch, and salt. Whisk till smooth.

2. Add milk in small splashes, whisking all along. Do not add it in a big pour.

3. Put pan on low to mid-low gas. Whisk without a stop, all around pan bottom and wall.

4. It will stay thin for a bit. Do not turn up gas. As it warms, it will go silky and thick.

5. If a big blob or puff pops up, lift pan off gas. Whisk hard for 30 s. Put it back on low gas and whisk for 1 min. It must look glossy, thick, and uniform, with no grainy bits.

6. Tip into a cool bowl. Put film onto its top. Chill.

If it starts to look grainy:

- Lift pan off gas right away.
- Whisk fast with 1 to 2 tbsp cold milk.
- If tiny lumps still stay, blitz till smooth.

## Custard, No Curdling

Two bad pans do not show poor skill. Go low, go slow, and whisk nonstop.

For a small batch:

- 300 g full-fat milk
- 3 yolks
- 60 g sugar
- 25 g cornflour
- 1 pinch salt
- 1 tsp vanilla

1. Put yolks, sugar, cornflour, and salt in a cool, solid pot. Whisk to a no-lump, silky mix.

2. Add milk in 4 small lots, whisking hard. Do not dump it all in at a go.

3. Put pot on low gas. Whisk nonstop, all around pot bottom and pot wall.

4. At first, it stays thin. Hold low gas. Do not rush with high gas.

5. As it starts to thicken, keep whisking. It should look glossy and coat a spoon.

6. On its first slow blip, pull pot off gas. Whisk for 30 to 60 s. Put back on low gas for 30 s, still whisking.

7. Pull off gas. Add vanilla and whisk. Tip into a cool bowl. Lay food film right on top. Chill.

If it starts to look grainy, pull it off gas at once and whisk in 1 tbsp cold milk. Whisk hard until smooth.

An eyepiece rarely gives the vivid, wide, bright scenes in advertising. Such images usually arise via lengthy camera runs, many stacked frames, filters, and digital edits. Human sight gathers little light in real time; thus faint deep-sky targets seem tiny, dim, and nearly gray. Urban glare, haze, air shimmer, and an unsteady instrument strip detail. High magnifying may yield a larger yet dimmer, shakier image.

Give sight 20–30 min in darkness; use a dark site; keep magnifying mild; use star charts. A rigid base and patient aiming matter greatly. Skill and repeated visits reveal finer detail.

Such targets are genuinely rich because each view is direct: ancient light reaches your retina, rather than a vivid image made by a camera. Expect subtle detail, then let familiarity reveal extra detail.

draft:
Star streaks are not a sign of bad kit. As Earth spins, stars slide across the sensor while an exposure is in progress. A long exposure records that slide as a line; a brief one records less of it, so stars stay closer to dots.

One no-cost fix is to set a briefer exposure. Start at 10 seconds, inspect the image at high magnification, and make it briefer if stars show lines. To keep the scene bright, raise ISO; this can add grain.

A second no-cost fix is to select a wider field of view. Set a zoom at its widest focal length, if it has one. At a wider view, each star’s drift spans fewer pixels, so the same drift is far less easy to see.

There is no way to make stars stay still in a long exposure with a fixed lens position: Earth keeps spinning. For very long exposures with dot-like stars, a tracking rig is needed, yet the two settings above cost nil.

draft:
Star trails happen because Earth spins. While a long time setting is active, each star moves a little across the image area. That motion is recorded as a line. At a brief time setting, there is less motion, so stars look more like dots.

Set a briefer time, perhaps 10 sec, then inspect the image. If stars still look long, cut the time again. Raise ISO if the image looks dim, though this may add grain.

Also, pick a wider angle of view. If a zoom lens is on hand, set it at its widest end. A wide view makes each star’s motion seem smaller, so trails are less easy to see.

draft:
A chimney sweep visit at a newly opened heat spot may go like this:

1. A look at the setup  
The sweep checks the opening, flue, pot, and stack, as safe access allows. This may show loose bits, a blocked flue, nest stuff, leaf build-up, wet signs, and an old cap.

2. Soot setup  
Dust sheets go below and about the opening. The opening has a taped soot hood, with a high-suction soot vac in place. This limits soot in the home.

3. The main sweep  
At the low end, linked poles with a whip head go up the flue. The head loosens soot, old nest bits, leaf bits, and thick black glaze. At times, a top-side method is used.

4. Clean-out and close look  
The vac lifts loose soot. A lamp, plus a video scope, can look along the flue to seek splits, gaps, loose joints, plus a bad flue tube. Big faults, blockages, and leak paths need a fix.

5. Smoke test  
A smoke pellet may be lit in the opening. The sweep sees if smoke heads up the flue, and if any leak shows in the loft, plus any adjoining space. This gives a good idea of flue pull.

6. Notes and next steps  
The sweep notes what was found, says if the flue looks fit to use, and gives upkeep tips. Get a dated job log and note any limits.

A clean flue is not a full safety sign-off. If this setup has no known past, ask a qualified solid-fuel fit-out tech to check flue size, air feed, heat-safe gaps, and the opening ahead of its initial use. Fit a CO safety unit and test it on its set cycle.

draft:
## Why the view is not like an online image

Many sky images add light bit by bit, using many minutes of light. A digital aid can mix this light and make dim hues easy to see. An eye takes in light only in a moment.

Thus dim gas clouds and faint galaxies look small, soft, and pale. Sky glow, haze, moonlight, bad focus, and a wobbly stand take away much detail. A big scope can aid, but it cannot make an eye view act like an image built up in many minutes.

## What to see

The Moon is a top aim. Its pits, hills, long dim plains, and lit cliff edges can look amazing. Aim along the line amid light and shade: low Sun makes shape stand out.

A big banded planet can show two main dim bands plus its 4 tiny moons. A planet with a wide, pale halo is also a fine sight. Venus has phases.

Pairs of tiny light points can look lovely, with unlike hues. A loose mass of many pinpoints can fill a low-magnification view. A dense ball of tiny light points can look like mist full of tiny points. M42, a gas cloud, can show a pale, misty glow at a dim-sky site.

## How to see much

Use low magnification. Let the scope cool off. Keep lamps out of sight; give eyes 20–30 min in low light. A steady stand and good aim have a big effect. Go to a site well away from city glow. Use a sky-map app in dim mode.

A good aim is not a photo. It is a live sight of a planet, a moon, a deep-sky object, seen with one's own eye. That can make a small, pale sight feel amazing.

draft:
## Why online images look unlike an eyepiece view

Many online images add light bit by bit over long spans. Digital tools can lift faint hues and tiny bits. An eye takes in only a small amount of light at any one time, so dim galaxies and nebulas tend to look pale, hazy, and small.

Sky glow, mist, moonlight, bad focus, and a shaky mount also cut what is seen. A big scope helps, yet no scope can make an eye view act like a long digital image.

## Good aims in an eyepiece

The Moon is a top aim. Look at its impact pits, hills, and wide plains. Aim at the line amid day and night: low Sun makes the land shape stand out.

A huge banded gas planet can show two main bands plus a set of small moons. A pale planet with a flat halo is also lovely. Venus shows phases.

Two close suns can look lovely. A loose group of many light points can fill a view. A tight ball of many points can look like a misty glow. M42 can show a pale, smoky patch in a good night sky.

## Ways to see more

Begin with low magnification. It gives a wide, calm view and makes aiming easy. Use a solid mount and focus well. Let the scope cool.

Hide local lamps. Give eyes 20–30 min with no white light. Go to a site well away from city glow. Use a sky-map app set to dim mode.

Look a little to one side of a faint object, not at its middle. This can make it stand out. Visit on many nights: skill builds with use.

A live sight has its own magic. A tiny pale patch can be a vast galaxy at an immense distance. Its light may have spent ages on its way to an eye.

draft:
No-split custard

Two bad runs do not doom this batch.

For 4 small pots

- 500 ml full-fat milk
- 4 yolks
- 75 g sugar
- 25 g cornstarch
- 1 pinch salt
- 1 tsp vanilla

1. Put yolks, sugar, cornstarch, salt, and vanilla in a cool bowl. Whisk till fully smooth.

2. Put milk in a pan. Warm it on low till hot, with wisps of vapor. No boiling.

3. Whisk yolk mix without a stop. Add a small mugful of hot milk in a thin flow. Whisk till smooth. Add an additional small mugful in a thin flow.

4. Tip bowl mix into pan. Put pan on low. Stir nonstop, all across pan bottom and around its sides.

5. As it turns thick, look for slow, soft blobs. At that point, pull pan off hob. Whisk hard for 30 to 60 s. Its own warmth will finish cooking it.

6. If still too thin, put pan back on low for 10 s, stirring all along. Pull it off again. Do this only if still thin.

7. Spoon into cups. To avoid a skin, lay food film on its top. Chill till cold.

Avoiding splits

- Low hob only.
- No boil.
- Cornstarch must go in at start.
- Stir nonstop as it turns thick.
- Pull pan off hob as soon as it turns thick.
- Do not walk off.
- If grainy bits show, pull pan off at once and whisk in 1 to 2 tbsp cold milk.

draft:
No-split custard

For 4 small pots

- 500 ml full-fat milk
- 4 yolks
- 75 g sugar
- 25 g cornstarch
- 1 pinch salt
- 1 tsp vanilla

1. Put yolks, sugar, cornstarch, salt, and vanilla in a cool bowl. Whisk until smooth.

2. Put milk in a pan. Warm on low until hot. Do not allow a boil.

3. While whisking yolk mix without stopping, add a small amount of hot milk in a thin flow. Whisk smooth. Add a bit more hot milk in a thin flow.

4. Tip all bowl mix into pan. Put pan on low. Stir nonstop, with whisk touching pan floor and wall.

5. When custard turns thick, pull pan off hob at once. Whisk hard for 1 min. Its own warmth will finish it.

6. If still thin, put pan back on low for 10 s, stirring all along. Pull it off. Do this only if still thin.

7. Put into pots. Lay film on top if you do not want a skin. Chill.

Tips

- Low hob only.
- Do not boil.
- Stir nonstop from start until thick.
- Pull pan off as soon as it turns thick.
- If tiny lumps show up, pull pan off at once and whisk in 1 to 2 tbsp cold milk.

At half pace, each note, finger, and shift can be seen and set. The mind links each action to the right result.

draft:
On an icy hill, use a calm, light touch.

1. Line up with lots of open space uphill.
2. Set the wheel as close to dead ahead as you can.
3. With a manual box, select 2, not 1. Let the clutch up bit by bit, then add only a hint of gas.
4. With an auto box, use snow mode if it has one. Ease onto the gas; do not jab it.
5. If a wheel begins to spin, lift off at once. Let it slow, then go once again with even less gas.
6. Keep the wheel still as you set off. Big wheel moves can make a slide.
7. Build slow, even speed. Do not stop midway up if you can avoid it.
8. If safe, put sand, salt, or a non-slip mat by the wheels that make it go. You may chip loose ice away if it is safe.

Stop and walk if:

- You slide side to side, or begin to go back downhill.
- Each go has wheel spin, or you gain no distance.
- You cannot see a safe way, or any autos may come close.
- The hill is too steep, or ice is thick, smooth, and solid.
- You do not feel at ease.

Stop only at a safe, legal spot well off any lane. Do not leave it in a lane. Seek aid if needed. If you get out, stay uphill of it and well away from its path.

An IHD gives a handy, near-live view of electricity use. It can:

- Show current use, usually in watts or kilowatts.
- Keep daily, weekly, and billing-period history.

- Help flag a large rise when a kettle, heater, dryer, etc. is started.

Select a lamp set made for wet, cold use. Look for an IPX6 or IPX7 mark, a sealed USB-C port, and no bare metal around the charge area. Favor a tough alloy or hard polymer case, a deep gasket, and a screw-on cap.

That outward flow forms when wave after wave leaves extra water near shore. The water seeks a low gap through a sandbar or another open path, then heads away from land. A strong, narrow outflow can move a person far from shore. The outflow does not pull a person below the surface; fear and hard work back toward shore are what make the event so hazardous.

From dry sand, watch for a darker, smoother lane among breaking surf, a gap where waves do not break as much, or foam, weed, and sand going away from shore. Such a lane may look calm, yet that calm patch can carry water outward. These marks are not always clear, so ask a beach guard about hazards before going out.

When caught, stay calm. Float on your back or tread water; do not battle the outflow by going straight toward shore. Raise one arm, call for help, and hold onto a board or other float when one can be had. When able, move along shore, not toward or away from land, to get clear of the fast lane. Then head back toward shore. When that move cannot be done, keep afloat, wave, and save energy for help. A strong swimmer can grow worn out fast, so calm acts matter more than raw power.

draft:
Photos can fool. A backyard optic is not a NASA imaging rig. Astro photos may stack many long runs and add digital work. A human optic can hold light for only a tiny instant, so a faint object stays a faint blur. Skyglow from towns cuts contrast. A small optic also hits limits from glass width, air motion, and mount jiggle.

Targets with high impact:

- Moon: sharp impact pits, mountain rims, and a shifting light-dark boundary  
- Saturn: a small oval with rings, on calm nights  
- Jupiter: two main cloud bands, plus four bright moons  
- Mars: a tiny rust disk during opposition  
- M42, in Orion: a luminous fog patch  
- M31: a dim oval glow in a rural, dark sky  
- M13: a grainy ball of stars  
- M45: a sparkling star group  

Do not hunt for photo color. At low light, human vision drops most color, so faint fogs look gray or bluish. That is normal, not a flaw.

Allow 20 to 30 min away from bright lamps. Use a dim ruby lamp if you must scan a sky map. Start at low magnification. High magnification can blow up an item, but it also dims it and magnifies air shimmer.

With skill, faint blurs gain form and story.

draft:
Getting uphill on ice

On ice, grip is low. Use smooth, tiny inputs, not speed.

Before you try

- If possible, pick different route or hold off until grit, tire socks, or other grip help is present.
- Keep wheels pointed uphill.
- Remove loose ice from in front of tires if risk is low.
- Do not begin if people, vehicles, or drop-offs lie below or close by.

To get moving

1. Use the highest gear still suited to moving off smoothly. In most stick-shift vehicles, use second. If gear choice exists, pick second or low-slip mode.
2. Ease clutch out very slowly, using only tiny engine input. With no clutch, press very softly.
3. Once moving, keep input even. Do not surge. Keep steering nearly still.
4. Keep slow, steady motion. Do not stop mid-slope.

If tires spin

- Lift your foot fully. Let tires quit spinning.
- Keep wheels straight.
- Retry with less engine input, or use higher gear.
- If spin still occurs, quit. More engine force will only polish ice.

When to quit, then go on foot

- You lose uphill motion twice.
- Vehicle slips to one side or points off route.
- You need engine input beyond tiny levels.
- You do not keep room from people, vehicles, or an edge.
- Your boots slip on ice.
- You do not know if route ends in level, open spot.

If you quit, get tow help. Secure vehicle: select P or low gear, then set its lever or foot hold control. Use lights or blinkers so others see it.

draft:
Why 10 min at 50% wins

At full clip, your hands may run on habit. If a slip occurs, you rush past it. Many runs can drill that slip in.

At 50%, you gain room to look, plan, and fix. You can:

- put all digits in right spots  
- link one part to a following part  
- hold a solid pulse  
- watch timing  
- stop at any snag and sort it out  

Skill grows from right, mindful runs, not just lots of runs. A slow, sound run puts a good map in your brain and hands. As you add a bit of zip, that map holds.

Try this:

1. Pick 1–2 bars.  
2. Play at 50%, with no slips.  
3. If a slip pops up, halt, find why, and drill that bit 3x.  
4. Do 3 good runs in a row.  
5. Add a small amount of zip only if all stays solid.  

This can do much for you, vs 10 fast runs. It builds control, accuracy, and calm. Full clip is for testing what is solid; slow work is for making it solid.

draft:
### Why a hive splits

A mature bee family may split, increasing its numbers. If usable nest area and empty cells fail, and queen scent plus bee-age mix fail in curbing swarm drive, bees rear new queens. The laying queen then flies away with many adult bees, leaving queen cells and many nest bees. This lets the hive persist with a virgin queen while its flying unit seeks a fresh nest.

### Signs in the 14 days ahead

- Male bees and male-cell areas rise, mainly at frame edges.
- Heavy nectar influx; egg-rearing space gets filled with saved feed, leaving scant empty cells and limiting queen laying.
- Frames sit thick with bees; linked chains appear; a beard hangs at hive face and beneath frames, mainly in heat.
- Egg laying wanes as bees slim the queen ahead of flight.
- Queen cups gain eggs, then larvae amid rich larval feed. Many charged queen cells sit near side and basal frame margins.
- Flight may occur near capping of queen cells.
- A spare super may stay nearly unused if tight packing sits amid egg-rearing space.
- The queen may appear lighter, faster, and less fully fed; bees may attend her less.

At 7-day intervals in spring, inspect every central frame. Charged queen cells give the clearest imminent signal. Add spare empty drawn frames while cups stay empty. If charged cells exist, an artificial split can mimic the event and limit flying swarms.

draft:
## Reserve plan

A reserve plan is a clear, written basis for deciding how much cash and other readily usable assets a charity aims to keep.

It sets out:

- the sum the charity needs
- the risks it is meant to meet
- when trustees may use it
- how and when it will be built up again
- any funds set aside for a stated aim

It helps trustees ensure the charity can pay bills, staff, grants, and vital activity if gifts fall, an asset fails, or an emergency hits.

The relevant state agency asks if trustees have this plan because charity assets exist for the charity’s aims. Trustees need a sound basis for keeping funds back, or for using spare funds rather than letting cash sit idle.

A plan lets trustees:

- assess financial risk
- explain their judgment
- act in a fair and timely way
- give funders and the public faith in the charity’s care

An absent plan is not always a breach. A tiny, stable charity may need little, or nil. Yet trustees still need a reasoned view, written down and revisited as risks, cash needs, and activity alter.

draft:
On ice, wheelspin removes grip. Use low torque, low speed, smooth inputs.

1. Keep tires in line. If possible, select 2nd before you begin; it limits torque. In self-shifting vehicles, use icy mode, if fitted.

2. For stick shift, lift clutch in tiny, slow steps. Use only enough right-foot input to move. In self-shifting vehicles, use very light right-foot input. Do not stomp or floor it.

3. If tires spin, lift off fully. Let them quit spinning, then retry with less input. More power will only reduce grip.

4. If you keep moving, hold steering nearly still; use tiny corrections. Do not stop on steep ice unless you must.

5. If room below is open, you could roll downhill slightly, then use mild motion to get uphill. Do this only if no person, vehicle, or object is below you.

Quit if tires spin on every try; if vehicle slips to one side; if you need more speed per try; if you could hit something; or if you do not see enough open room.

If you quit, stop only in low-risk spot. In self-shifting type, set P. In stick shift, select 1st or R. Get help, or go on foot if doing so is less risky.

Surf sends huge volumes in. Those volumes must then return. Return flow often focuses through low cuts in submerged ridges, producing swift, focused offshore jets. It chiefly moves you out, not under. Risk comes from tiring yourself, cold, or being pushed into violent surf.

A day-case means you come to a care centre, have the planned procedure, rest as staff check you, then go home that same day. The team can tell you about food or water rules, what to wear, what to bring, and what meds to take or leave out.

**Who to call**

Keep the aftercare sheet and phone no. close. For normal concerns, ring the ward or care team named on that sheet. For urgent trouble, such as heavy blood loss, breath trouble, fever, or you are hard to wake, call your local emergency number.

**Road use**

Do not take the wheel after any drug that makes you sleepy. Have an adult take you home and stay near you for the rest of the day. Most often, 24 hours must pass before you take the wheel, yet follow the care team’s own rule.

draft:
Fair plot-list plan

Aim

Run a list by rules known at start. Apply one path to all. Log all actions. Allow any applicant to know rank and why.

1. Put policy in writing

- Say who may join, how to join, what facts to supply, and how rank works.
- Use order of first logging. Log any form on arrival, with day and clock mark to 1/60 of an hour.
- If two forms carry same clock mark, draw lots in sight of two impartial folk, and log that draw.
- List all lawful priority rules. Only apply a priority rule if a local law, funding contract, or plot group's constitution calls for it.
- Do not add informal favours.
- Say what occurs if an applicant says no, cannot take a plot, or is quiet.

2. Make list public, guard data

- Assign each applicant a random tag.
- Publish tag, rank, join day, and status: waiting, plot call, on hold, or off-list.
- Do not put full ID, mail info, or contact info in public.
- If an applicant asks, supply rank, policy, and any log item about that applicant.

3. Fill plots by rank

- On a vacant plot, call first waiting applicant.
- Try two contact paths, such as a call plus mail.
- Allow 7 days for a word.
- If no word by day 7, mark a pass.
- A pass must follow policy: rank may stay, go on hold, or go to tail.
- Do not skip rank for a pal, a donor, or an official.
- An odd plot may call for a willing applicant who can work it; list this option in policy, and log it.

4. Keep list alive

- At a 12-month point, ask all waiting folk to confirm.
- Try same contact path and same final day for all.
- If no word, mark off-list. Say how an applicant may join again, and if old rank is lost.
- No backdating following a gap if policy did not allow it from start.

5. Guard against bias

- One official logs all shifts; a co-chair audits it.
- Log day, old rank, rank now, cause, and initials.
- No official may shift a family or pal application solo.
- Allow a complaint within 14 days.
- An official with no part in that action looks at logs and posts a ruling.
- Hold a monthly audit. Audit list rank, plot calls, pass marks, and odd shifts.

6. Show facts and policy shifts

- Monthly, post total waiting count, plots vacant, plots now full, and typical wait in months.
- Do not post applicant data.
- Post any policy shift 30 days prior to its start.
- Adopt shifts by a group ballot, with a log.

Why this can win trust

Known rules, a public rank list, lot draws for same-clock arrivals, full logs, no solo shifts, and a complaint path all cut suspicion.

draft:
## Why an optic falls short

A sky optic is not a camera. Human vision soaks up light for only a short span, so faint forms look gray, small, and low in contrast. Long camera runs can add light from many shots, pull out color, and boost contrast. Publicity shots may also crop, smooth, or push color hard.

Air glow, city light, poor focus, a shaky mount, and a small optic all limit what you spot. A dark rural sky and a good long wait for vision to adapt can do much that a costly optic cannot. Avoid bright lamps for 30 min; a dim ruby lamp is a smart aid.

Start with bright, bold sights:

- Moon: crags, pits, walls, and long shadows along its light-dark rim.
- Saturn: its ring, plus Titan on a calm night.
- A Jovian giant: cloud bands and four big moons. Watch a moon's black dot cross its disk.
- Mars: a tiny bright disk; dark marks may show on a calm night.
- Dawn or dusk star: its changing lit form.

draft:
Why the eyepiece differs from the ads

A telescope does not make the sky look like a space-agency image. It gathers more light than an eye, yet an eyepiece gives a small, dim scene. Most famed galaxies and glowing gas regions are faint, and eyes see little color in low light. Cameras can collect light for a long time, then stack and edit many frames. Those images show real detail, yet they are not the instant eye view.

A city sky, haze, moonlight, shaky air, poor dark adaptation, and excessive magnification can all dim an image. A bigger lens or mirror helps, yet a modest scope at a dark site can beat a vast scope beneath city glare. Let eyes adapt in darkness for perhaps 20 to 30 min, and avoid white light. Start at low power, set a crisp image, and let the target drift across the field. Good seeing matters most for planets.

There is still a great deal to see. The Moon is an ideal first target: craters, rims, shadows, and bright ray patterns can look sharp, even from a town. At low power, scan the Pleiades, the Beehive, and rich star fields; star gatherings can seem like spilled diamonds. Orion’s bright haze can show a pale gray-green mist in a dark sky. The Andromeda galaxy appears as a soft oval glow, impressive less for color than for the fact that its light has crossed immense space.

The striped giant planet can show main belts and four bright moons. The ringed planet can show its rings. Mars can reveal a tiny disk near a fine opposition. A bright inner planet can show phases. Paired stars, like Albireo, give fine color contrast.

Set hopes for a calm kind of wonder rather than a postcard. Learn the sky, revisit targets as seasons shift, and note what eyes see and what a camera records. The first clear sight of the ringed planet or the striped giant’s four moon points can carry more impact than any image, since it is live light arriving at that moment.

Why this kills run:

If all on board rush up to catch, a lot of body mass is flying along rails. At catch, that mass must halt fast. It pulls against hull and adds a sharp jolt, as if hull has run into its own cargo. Oars may also go in amid this jolt, so foot push cannot link up as one solid hit.

On a good way back, body mass rolls toward catch with no rush. It is smooth, calm, and in sync. Just prior to catch, all slow as one; oars drop in, and foot push starts. Hull has room to run.

With good timing, hull slips on its own, with a long, light lull on way to catch. You wait for catch; catch rolls up to you. At push, all oars lock on right away, and hull jumps.

draft:
Reserves policy

It is written outline of funds kept for future use. It tells trustees:

- its purpose  
- desired sum or level  
- method used to set it  
- which funds count  
- where those funds sit  
- when review occurs  
- steps if levels drop or rise  

Why it helps

When income dips, bills come due, or unexpected costs hit, reserves let nonprofit keep crucial work going. Reserves could cover rent, employee costs, core bills, short disruption, or orderly closure if needed. Only funds free for trustee use count, unless donor terms permit use.

Why oversight body seeks it

The body which supervises nonprofits keeps seeking this because it needs to see trustees know risks, use funds properly for intended public benefit, plus hold neither too much nor too little.

Too much could suggest funds sit idle despite no defined purpose. Too little could disrupt services. It also gives donors, funders, plus service users reason to trust trustee control. No single sum fits every nonprofit, so it looks for sensible reasons, not one fixed rule.

How to produce one

Use budget, risk list, cost commitments, debt, insurance, income timing, plus intended work. Set desired level, often in number of months of core spending. Record reasons in policy.

Trustees should approve it, review it once per 12-month period, plus revise it if income, costs, or work shift. Put short note in periodic report, so readers know its purpose, level, plus review process.

Earth spins. Thus, during a lengthy camera capture, stars shift within each pixel area. A fixed camera then renders each star as a faint line, rather than a crisp pinprick.

To build a lasting oil skin on cast iron, scrub off rust or old food with hot water and a stiff brush. Dry at once, then warm pan on a hot cooktop until all damp is gone. Rub a tiny amount of flax, soy, or corn oil all around pan, including its long arm. Rub again with a dry cloth until no oily gloss is in sight. Put pan bottom-up in a hot grill or BBQ for about an hour, allow it to cool, and run this 2 or 3 rounds.

Oil, amid strong warmth, forms a hard, dark coating that sticks to iron. First 3 cooking runs do not lock in a pan's long story. Mild fatty cooking in that span can start a solid coating, but any run can add to it or harm it. Skip long acidic cooking and harsh scouring at first. If food sticks, add oil and carry on; cast iron can always gain a good skin again.

draft:
Silky stovetop egg mix

You need:
- 500 ml full-fat milk
- 6 egg yolks
- 100 g white sweet bits, as sold for tea
- 1 tsp vanilla
- a tiny bit of salt

1. Set out a whisk, pan, ladle, sieve, and two bowls. Fill one bowl with ice and cold tap H2O. Set the second bowl in it.

2. Add milk, vanilla, and salt to the pan. Heat on low. Stop when steam lifts off it and tiny bubbles show at the pan side. Do not let it boil.

3. In a bowl, beat yolks and sweet bits until smooth.

4. Whisk yolks nonstop. Add hot milk a little at a time. Add one small ladle, whisk well, then add one more. Keep going until all milk is in.

5. Tip all of it back into the pan. Set heat to low. Use a silicone spatula to keep it moving, with slow sweeps all along the pan base and sides.

6. Do not let it boil. Stop when it coats a spoon and a line made with a clean nail on the back of the spoon stays open. If you use a heat tool, aim for 80 to 82 C.

7. At once, pass it via the sieve into the bowl on ice. Mix now and then until cool.

Key points:
- Low heat only.
- No big bubbles.
- Whisk as hot milk goes into yolks.
- Do not walk off once it is back on heat.
- If tiny egg bits show, take it off heat at once and pass it via the sieve.

This is colony reproduction. In spring, worker numbers rise quickly, brood fills much of nest, drones develop, plus honey flow begins. If open comb is short, or old-queen odor does not spread well through crowded nest, workers begin to produce new queens. The old queen then quits with lots of workers, letting one new queen rule those left.

Over prior fortnight, inspect for thick bee cover over most comb, bees clumped below inner cover, few open cells for eggs or new food, drone brood, queen cups, then queen cells holding eggs or tiny grubs. You could see fewer eggs from old queen, since workers feed her less so she gets light enough to fly. Bees could pour round entry or form outside clump in hot, still conditions.

The strongest clue is sealed queen cells. Exit commonly occurs close to when first cell is sealed, though cool or wet conditions can defer it. Weekly spring checks help. Give empty built comb or extra box early, reduce brood-box crowding, or split colony when queen cells show firm intent. Merely cutting queen cells seldom fixes root issue; workers often build more.

draft:
Swarming is how honey bee colonies multiply. In spring, brood reering speeds up, worker numbers rise, drones emerge, plus incoming pollen or honey fills comb. If room for brood, pollen, or honey is too low, or if queen scent no longer moves through the huge bee cluster well, workers begin queen cells for new queen. They slim the old queen by giving her less food, so she is fit for flight. Then she exits, joined by numerous workers, leaving brood, stores, plus developing queen cells behind.

In the two weeks prior to queen exit, you could see congestion: bees cover most comb, cells in which queen puts eggs grow few, plus drones or drone brood become common. Little queen cups, often on lower comb edges, then hold eggs, milk-white young, or rich white food. Soon, long tube-like queen cells grow. Once workers put wax lids over such cells, swarm risk is very high; old queen often goes soon, if skies permit.

Other hints include bees hanging in thick clumps under inner cover or on hive front, especially in hot periods. The queen could put fewer eggs owing to slimming. Inspect weekly in spring. Give room early: put in built comb, give upper box room, or divide colony when queen-cell work shows strong swarm intent. Simply removing queen cells seldom solves it, since bees frequently build more.

A calm way to lead a long call

Keep a calm tone. Do not cut in or talk on top of them. When a small gap comes, say:

I can see this is a lot. So I can help, may I ask one key thing now?

I want to make good use of this call. Can we look at what you need most today?

So, you feel this has been a lot. Is that it?

draft:
Committee guide

Use this system so people see an even, open process.

1. Keep one public, written queue.
2. Log every request in time order. Give every person one ID.
3. Post order, rules, plot types, fees, plus likely queue time. Keep phone, home, plus other private info off public view.
4. Use one fixed offer rule. When plot opens, offer it to first eligible ID for its size or type.
5. Set eligibility before use: residence link, membership, one-plot limit, plus other rules your group uses. Use them for everyone.
6. Give every person one reply limit: seven full 24-hour periods. Send offer by electronic post, plus post if needed. Keep proof.
7. If person declines, gives no reply, or no longer fits rules, record reason then move to next ID. Do not drop them unless published rules permit it. Let them keep or lose their spot by one known rule.
8. Let people revise contact info or plot wish without jumping queue.
9. Log every offer, reply, skip, plus result. Keep log for review.
10. Put two or more people in every key step, so no one person shifts order.
11. Review list once per month. Correct errors in public, with old plus new entry shown.
12. Offer short route for disputes: written request, review by people not in first decision, then written result.
13. For tied requests, use preset lots with observers. Record result.
14. Do not give unseen priority to friends, donors, or committee members. If priority groups exist, list them openly. Use strict limits.
15. Give every 12-month report: number on list, offers, declines, plus rule edits. Tell people before rule edits begin.

Keep rules brief, public, plus fixed. If rules need edits, use new rules only for future requests. This gives one visible order, one rule set for everyone, proof, plus review.

Run it by these rules:

Sill-grown seedlings often become long, thin, pale, if light is too low. Low light prompts shoots to lengthen in pursuit of stronger light. This uses stored food, so stems end up weak, while new growth forms less green pigment. Warm rooms, wet potting mix, or crowding worsen it.

Before next sowing, use LED grow lights from first sprout. Keep lights close to pots, with room so shoots do not touch. Lift lights bit by bit while shoots rise. Run them for fourteen to sixteen h within each full twenty-four-hour cycle. Sow seeds thinly in light, free-flowing compost. Keep it moist, not wet. Give seedlings room; keep them cool. If only sill light is on offer, pick your brightest sill, turn pots often, or sow in spring, once outdoor light is stronger.
